sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: go build → the static binary (CGO_ENABLED=0) → scp to the server → systemd unit (Restart=always) or a process manager. The binary is self-contained: no runtime, no dependencies.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The build-and-deploy:

```bash
# Build the static binary
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -ldflags="-s -w" -o myapp .
# -s -w: strip debug info — smaller binary

# Copy to the server
scp myapp user@server:/opt/myapp/myapp

# The systemd unit (/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service)
[Unit]
Description=My Go App
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/myapp/myapp
Environment=PORT=8080
Restart=always
User=app

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# Enable and start
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
sudo systemctl status myapp
journalctl -u myapp -f     # the logs
```

The Go advantage this question tests: the binary is a single static file — no JVM, no Python interpreter, no node_modules, no runtime dependencies to install on the target. Copy one file, run one process. This is Go's deployment story.

The systemd features (the production requirements): Restart=always (crash → automatic restart — the resilient process); Environment (the config); User (the non-root security); After=network.target (the dependency ordering); journalctl (the log integration).

The binary's self-sufficiency: CGO_ENABLED=0 → no libc — runs on ANY Linux (distro, version); the Go runtime and the net stack are linked in. The 15MB single file is the entire deployment artifact.

The upgrade path (the production dance): build the new binary → scp it as myapp.new → the health check → mv myapp.new myapp → systemctl restart myapp — a brief downtime; the zero-downtime version (the socket handoff) or the blue-green (two instances behind a LB) are the scale-up.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B[CGO_ENABLED=0 go build] --> S[static binary ~15MB]
    S --> SCP[scp to server]
    SCP --> SYS[systemd unit]
    SYS --> RUN[Restart always]
    SYS --> ENV[Environment config]
    SYS --> LOG[journalctl logs]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The systemd unit's production tuning (the interview's depth layer): RestartSec=5 (the backoff between restarts — a crash-loop at 0 delay is a CPU burner); LimitNOFILE (the file descriptors — a Go server with many connections); WorkingDirectory (relative paths); Environment= or EnvironmentFile=/opt/myapp/env (the config file — the secret separation).

The zero-downtime graceful handoff (Go's specific capability): the new process inherits the listening socket (systemd's FD passing or the SO_REUSEPORT trick), the old process stops accepting, finishes in-flight, exits. Go's http.Server.Shutdown + the socket-inheritance is the deployment story without a load balancer.

The binary-vs-container decision, honestly: the binary alone (the scp+systemd path) is Go's heritage deployment — smallest, simplest, the single-artifact advantage. The container adds: the same artifact everywhere (the image layers include the runtime environment: certs, timezone), the orchestrator's lifecycle (Kubernetes' health probes, rolling updates), and the standardized pipeline. The modern default is the container; the bare binary remains the fall-back and the proof of Go's self-containment.
